On the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Sitaram is the guard blocking Udayaditya’s way: he obeys the Maharaj’s orders, tries to prevent Udayaditya from leaving, and only lets him pass after Udayaditya threatens him and Sitaram asks to be disarmed and bound. On the night of Udayaditya’s own escape, Sitaram reverses that role: he opens the prison door, claims the prison is on fire, physically takes Udayaditya out, and leads him away. The guard who once restrained Udayaditya becomes the one who frees and guides him.

Pratapaditya’s first plan was to have two Pathan men kill Basanta Ray on the road to Jessore, near the inn at Simultali. The plan failed because one of the Pathans could not bring himself to commit the murder and instead confessed the plot to Basanta Ray and Udayaditya.

Basanta Ray’s life finally ends when Pratapaditya sends Muktiyar Khan with a signed order for the death sentence of the King of Raigarh. Muktiyar Khan enters the fort, presents the order to Basanta Ray, and then calls Abdul, who kills Basanta Ray with a sword.
In the inner quarters of the Jessore palace, where he had entered disguised as a woman; and in the king’s chamber, where he was openly present as the jester, not in disguise.
The Rajmahishi secretly has Matangini fetch a poison/medicine prepared by Mangala (Rukmini), and Surma takes it, causing her death.

Vibha’s refusal is treated as a grave insult to Ramchandra Ray, leading him to marry another wife; when Vibha later reaches Chandradwip, she finds she has no place in her husband’s kingdom and her hopes of happiness are shattered.

Rukmini obtains Udayaditya’s ring, which has the Yubaraj’s name engraved as a seal. Bhagavat and Sitaram use it to stamp a forged petition supposedly sent by Udayaditya to the Emperor accusing Pratapaditya of treason. Bhagavat then presents this petition to Pratapaditya as if it had been intercepted from Udayaditya’s servant, and Pratapaditya uses it as grounds to imprison Udayaditya.

Ramchandra Ray’s midnight escape led to the guards who had been overpowered or forced to open the gates being dismissed. Udayaditya, feeling responsible, gave them a monthly stipend; Pratapaditya forbade this. Surma then secretly continued the stipends through a maid. When word reached Pratapaditya, he ordered Surma to be sent to her paternal home.

The song expresses Basanta Ray’s grief, loneliness, and sense of loss: the people he once loved and sang for are gone, joy has become empty, and he feels left alone in old age. He sings it first alone on his veranda in Raigarh at sunset, humming it spontaneously in private melancholy; later he sings it slowly in Jessore while holding Vibha’s hand in the silent, empty household, lamenting the broken family and Udayaditya’s imprisonment.

Rukmini fails to stop Udayaditya’s midnight escape, so he reaches Raigarh under Basanta Ray’s protection. Later, Rukmini tells Pratapaditya that Udayaditya escaped with Basanta Ray and Sitaram; Pratapaditya then sends Muktiyar Khan with a signed order to capture Udayaditya and execute the King of Raigarh, and Muktiyar Khan kills Basanta Ray.

Pratapaditya initially receives Ramchandra Ray with cool indifference and minimal ceremonial respect: he does not arrange a grand welcome, sends only a small welcoming party, and meets him without joy or haste, even turning away to attend to state business. This makes Ramchandra feel insulted and inferior. Later, however, Ramchandra reverses this dynamic in his own court by openly belittling Pratapaditya’s status, mocking his lineage, claiming that Pratapaditya’s family is inferior to his own, and treating the marriage as something that elevates Pratapaditya rather than the other way around.

She reappears in Jessore as Mangala, having left Raigarh and changed her name; she lives on the outskirts, wins over palace servants, and when the Rajmahishi secretly sends for her tantric medicine to win Udayaditya back from Surma, she prepares poison that causes Surma’s death.

His early lament—that he never wanted to be crown prince, was unfit to rule, and had been judged and despised by his father and court—culminates when, after being brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he accepts his father’s judgment that he is unworthy, asks to be released from the throne, and swears before Ma-Kali that he will never accept any part of Jessore’s kingdom, will not sit on its throne or touch its scepter, and that Samaraditya will be the heir; he then leaves for Kashi to live as an ascetic.

Nayanchand, afraid of Pratapaditya’s reaction, does not deliver the letter to him but gives it to the Mahishi; later, after Basanta Ray reads it, the Mahishi and Basanta Ray tell Vibha and the household that Ramchandra has written requesting that Vibha be sent to her in-laws’ house, turning the spiteful renunciation into a loving summons.

Pratapaditya tries to trap Ramchandra Ray by blocking the palace canal with large sal-wood logs, but the escape fails because Rammohan and his followers pull the boat up and over the logs, while the guards waste time finding a gun and fetching a chase boat, allowing the boat to escape to the Bhairav river.

Basanta Ray’s relationship with his sitar reflects his growing despair because the sitar, once his “eternal companion” and a source of music and joy, becomes something he can no longer bear to play. In Chapter 13, he leaves the sitar behind and says he will not play it anymore; when he tries to play it, his tears and distress over Udayaditya’s suffering stop him. In Chapter 27, he says the sitar is there but its strings are broken and it cannot be tuned, showing that his inner joy and emotional strength have been shattered. His inability to play or sing freely mirrors his helplessness and grief over Udayaditya’s imprisonment and separation from him.

Earlier, Udayaditya was known for his courage and willingness to intervene in the affairs of his subjects, even acting against oppression without considering the consequences. After Surma’s death, however, a blind fear of Pratapaditya takes hold of him: his courage disappears, he hesitates, avoids helping oppressed subjects, and no longer intervenes as he once would have.

He helps Udayaditya escape from prison—during the fire, Sitaram enters the prison, claims it is burning, and carries Udayaditya out into the open, undoing the imprisonment caused by the forged petition.

On the first occasion, Rammohan makes a rope from thick sheets, ties it to a pillar on the palace roof, carries Ramchandra Ray on his back, climbs down the rope, lowers Ramchandra into the boat in the canal, and then jumps down himself.

On the second occasion, after Vibha faints, Rammohan lifts her, carries her out of the palace, places her unconscious body into a palanquin near the gate, and takes her back to the boat.

In Jessore, Vibha is dressed as a richly adorned royal princess: she is made to wear eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring, and an elaborate hairstyle imposed by the Mahishi. Her appearance is ornate, proud, and ceremonial, meant to receive Ramchandra Ray with royal dignity.

In Chandradwip, her presentation is radically reversed. She refuses a palanquin, saying she is not a queen but will go “like a common subject, like a beggar-woman.” She is dressed as a common woman, her veil falls, and she enters the palace like a maidservant, unnoticed and unwelcomed. Ramchandra Ray even mistakes her for a beggar woman seeking alms. Thus, she shifts from being lavishly adorned as a princess to appearing plain, humble, and almost beggar-like.

In his bedchamber after Surma’s death, the window is tied to memory, loss, and longing: Udayaditya sits there expecting to see Surma, and it becomes a place where her absence is felt most sharply. In the prison cell, the window changes into a symbol of hope and freedom: through it he sees the sky and birds, and it makes him feel that he is still naturally free and that his imprisonment will one day end.

Sitaram first approaches Rukmini (Mangala) as a moneylender he can charm: he borrows cash from her, flatters her with verses and endearing names, and treats the loan as part of a flirtatious relationship. His affection is tied to her “beauty and silver,” and he quickly turns the exchange into playful banter, though he angers her by asking about interest. He then fails to repay her and keeps returning, while their relationship becomes more secretive and strained.

After Udayaditya’s imprisonment, Sitaram’s attitude turns openly hostile: he curses Rukmini, threatens to burn her house, and vows to humiliate her. Rukmini, in turn, becomes fiercely possessive and vengeful, declaring that Udayaditya is “her” Yubaraj and that Sitaram will not succeed.

The final break occurs when Sitaram, having helped fake Udayaditya’s death in a fire, assumes Rukmini is dead and goes to rob her house. Instead, he finds her alive, trembling and soaked, and she threatens to kill him, saying she will burn him and Udayaditya and then take her own revenge. When she goes to fetch a curved blade, Sitaram realizes the danger and flees, turning their once flirtatious financial arrangement into a life-threatening confrontation.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse fire as a distraction: the huts near the prison catch fire, the guards abandon their posts to save their belongings, and the resulting chaos allows Sitaram to enter the prison and take Udayaditya away. The fire is not left as a mere diversion; Sitaram’s men deliberately worsen it by sabotaging the firefighting effort. Then they set fire to Udayaditya’s empty prison cell, making it appear that he is trapped inside. To complete the cover-up, Sitaram throws bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword into the burning cell, while others spread cries that the Yubaraj screamed and that the roof collapsed. This creates the false impression that Udayaditya died in the fire, concealing his actual escape.

He interprets Udayaditya’s protection as something that was simply expected and done mainly for his own sister’s sake, not out of genuine loyalty to Ramchandra Ray; in court, Ramchandra Ray shows no gratitude and instead joins in mocking Udayaditya as Pratapaditya’s son.

Pratapaditya’s dismissal of the Emperor of Delhi is turned against his son when Bhagavat and Sitaram forge a petition, stamped with the Yubaraj’s seal, supposedly sent to Delhi accusing Pratapaditya of treason. Bhagavat presents it to Pratapaditya as a captured appeal by Udayaditya’s servant, making the son appear to have invoked the Emperor’s authority against his father; Pratapaditya then uses that alleged appeal to Delhi as the charge for punishing and imprisoning him.

The grooming of Vibha’s hair marks Surma’s presence as an intimate, caring act: when the Mahishi forces Vibha into an unwanted hairstyle, Vibha secretly goes to Surma, who styles her hair to her own liking. This shows Surma’s closeness to Vibha and her role as someone who understands and comforts her. After Surma’s tragic absence, the same hair ritual becomes a sign of loss: when it is time to braid her hair, Vibha sits waiting for Surma, but she never comes, and Vibha’s hair remains unbraided. Later, Vibha’s unkempt hair also reflects her grief and the absence of Surma’s care.
